ch.t: Chapter One. The Word I Gave
p: Chapter One. The Word I Gave

Not the thin kind you tie a parcel with. Ship rope. Thick as my wrist, brown as bread crust, heavy with tar. Our storehouse in York smelled of it — tar and hemp and dust — and I hated that smell the way only a boy of eighteen can hate a smell.
Every morning he counted the coils. Every evening he counted them again.
"Robinson," he said once, without looking up, "a man who counts his rope will never drown."
I thought it was the stupidest thing I had ever heard.
I was wrong. I paid for being wrong on an island with no name, four thousand miles from anyone who knew mine. But that comes later.
First you should know this. My father asked me for one thing. I gave him my word. I broke it before the month was out.
My father counted the coils every morning, and every evening he counted them again.
Our name was not really Crusoe.

My father came out of Bremen as a young man, and the name he carried was Kreutznaer, and York could not say it. So York filed it down the way a river files down a stone, and by the time I was born we were Crusoe, and no one remembered otherwise.
I have thought about that a great deal since. A name is not as fixed a thing as a boy imagines. Put it in enough strange mouths and it will come back to you changed.
York is not a sea town. But the Ouse runs down to Hull, and Hull opens on the whole grey world. Every rope my father sold went down that river to be tied to something that floated.
I used to walk to the staith and watch the barges load.

Twice a year he took me to Hull to see the chandlers, and those two days were the only days of my year. The forest of masts. The stink and shout of it. Men off ships from Danzig and Lisbon and places I could not have found on a map, all of them loud, all of them going somewhere.
My father knew that about me. That was the trouble.
The elder was a soldier. He was killed at Dunkirk, in a trench, at twenty-three. We know the date of it because a lieutenant wrote to us.
He was seventeen when he went and we never heard one word after, not from a port, not from a shipmate, not ever. He simply stopped.
We have no grave for either of them. For one we have a date. For the other we do not even have that.

After that my father stopped speaking about the sea the way other men in York spoke about it. To them it was a road. It was a living. It was the ordinary way a thing gets from one place to another. For him it stopped being a road. It became a mouth.
He tried to give me two things that year. I took neither.

The first was the counting. Every coil, every morning, every evening, and the number set down in a ledger in his small square hand. I told him a boy could learn nothing from a rope but how to be bored.
The second he gave me on the roof of the storehouse.
It was late, and cold, and I wanted to be asleep. He made me stand facing out over the dark town and he pointed north, at the star that does not move.
"Find that," he said. "Then you can find everything else."

He showed me how to hold my hand up against the sky and measure. He showed me how the star stood higher in the north and lower in the south. A man who watched it carefully could tell how far he had come. He made me do it four nights running and write the figures down.
"You will not always be in a place that tells you where you are," he said. "One day you may have to know it without being told."
I said yes, father. I said it three times. I looked at the star. And I thought about a ship I had seen at Hull, with a green hull and a crew of Portuguese.
I remembered almost none of it.
And I did not know then that I would one day use that star to find something other than my way home.
"Find that," he said. "Then you can find everything else."
The trouble came in the shape of a friend of mine, who had a face that could talk anyone into anything.
His father owned a share in a vessel going down to London on the first of the month, and she was short one man.
"Not one man," he said. "One boy. They want a boy who can write."
"They want a boy who can write and reckon and keep a cargo list. There is not one on the whole quay at Hull. Every boy on that quay was raised to haul and not to read."

And there it was. My father had made me a boy with ink on his fingers. I could count a hundred coils and set the number down in a straight line. That was exactly the thing that could buy me a place on a ship.
He had built the door himself. He just never thought I would find the handle.
He asked me for my word on a Thursday.
He had heard something. York is a small city for a secret. He did not shout at me, which I had been ready for. He put down the ledger, and he looked at me for a long time, and then he said:
"Give me your word that you will not go."
I could have said no. He would have shouted then, and I could have shouted back, and I could have walked out through a door I had kicked open honestly.
Instead I said, "I give you my word."

I have turned that moment over more times than I can count. I did not lie because I was afraid of him. I lied because it was easier, and because I had already decided, and because a promise seemed to me then like a thing made out of breath.
He nodded. He picked up the ledger again. And — this is the part I cannot get out of my head — he looked relieved.
I went down to Hull on the last day of August.

I told my mother I was going about a debt at the tannery. She gave me bread and cheese for the walk. She told me to give her greeting to a man named Wilkin, whom I had no intention of greeting. And she said what she always said, which was that I should be back before dark.
I took my own savings, which were small and honestly mine.
And I took one thing that was not.
From the back of the storehouse, where the short lengths lay that were too small to sell, I took a coil of my father's rope. Twenty feet of it. Good hemp, well laid, tarred the winter before.

I have never been able to explain why. I did not need it. I have thought since that I wanted to carry something of his out through that door. I would not carry the two things he had actually tried to give me.
It is the only thing I ever stole in my life.
It is also the reason I am alive to write this down.
There was a man standing at the end of the pier.
We went out on the first of September, in the year 1651, on the morning tide.
I stood at the rail and watched Hull turn from a town into a shape.
The steeples went first, then the roofs, then everything but the long grey line of the pier with the surf breaking white along it.
There was a man standing at the end of the pier.

He was too far off. He was a stroke of dark against the grey, no taller than my thumbnail. I could not have sworn to his face in front of any judge in the world. There are fishermen out there every morning of the year.
But he did not move, and he did not turn, and he was still standing there when the shape of him went into the haze.
I did not raise my hand.
I have had a great many years to think about that, and I still cannot tell you why.
I was sick before we cleared the river.

Nobody told me it would be like that. In my head I had been standing at the bow with the wind in my face, going somewhere. What actually happened was that I lay in the scuppers with my mouth open. I brought up bread and cheese until there was nothing left to bring up. Then I went on bringing up nothing.
I thought I was dying. I remember being almost glad about it.
What I could not forgive was that nobody cared.

Men stepped over me. One of them, going past with a coil on his shoulder, said "First time," in the voice you would use to say that it looked like rain. That was the whole of the sympathy I got in eleven hours.
I understand it now. Every man on that deck had lain where I was lying, once. To them I was not suffering. I was arriving.
By evening the sky and the water were the same colour.
By the second morning I was well, and by the second noon I was insufferable.

The wind was fair, the sea was long and easy, and the ship went over it the way a hand goes over a table. I stood at the rail with salt drying on my face and I thought: this is it, then. This is the thing my father was so frightened of.
I decided he was an old man who had been unlucky twice and had built a wall out of it.
I want to be fair to myself. I was eighteen. Nobody is sensible at eighteen.
But I want to be fair to him too. So I will say plainly what I thought, standing there, with the coast of my own country going by on the left hand. I thought I was better than him.
The wind began to rise on the fourth day, and it did not stop rising.

That is the part I cannot get people to understand. A storm at sea is not a thing that arrives. It is a thing that keeps arriving. Every hour it is worse than the hour before. Every hour you tell yourself that surely now it has done its worst. And every hour the sea shows you that you have no idea what its worst is.
By evening the sky and the water were the same colour and there was no line between them.

We ran in behind Yarmouth and let go both anchors with the rest of the shipping. There were a dozen sail in the Roads, all of us riding it out, all of us pitching. I could see the men on the nearest ship standing at their rail. They were looking at us exactly the way I was looking at them.
The mate came past me and I asked him if it was bad.
I have never in my life wanted so badly for a man to lie to me.
I made my vow at about two in the morning.

I had my arms around a stanchion and my face against the wood and the whole world was tipping. Green water came over the waist and went out through the ports. Somewhere below me something heavy had got loose and was going from side to side with a noise like a door being knocked down, over and over.
And I said — out loud, though nobody could have heard me — that if I were let live, I would go home.
Not next year. Not after one more voyage.
Home, on my own two feet, up the street to the storehouse door. I would say what I had done. And I would stand there while it was said back to me.
I meant it. That is the thing. People suppose a man in a storm does not mean it. I have never meant anything more.
They cut away the foremast to ease her.
At first light the cable parted.

I did not know what had happened. I only knew that the motion changed, and that men began running who had not been running before. The master came out of the roundhouse with his hair flat to his head. He started giving orders in a voice like a hammer.
We were dragging. Then we were dragging faster.

They cut away the foremast to ease her. I watched a man go up with an axe in weather that should have taken him off the ship and I thought, quite clearly: I could not do that. Not for any money. Not to save my own life.
She came upright a little when the mast went. It bought us maybe an hour.
Then the carpenter came up out of the hold and did not say anything to anybody, only went straight to the master, and after that they fired the gun.
I did not know what the gun meant either. I learned. It means: we are going down, and any boat that can reach us should come.

I will not pretend I remember it well. I remember the rope in my hands, and that the rope was wet. I remember that the drop from our rail to their thwart kept changing by about six feet. Up and down, up and down. And I had to choose the moment myself, because nobody had time to choose it for me.
I remember thinking, with a sort of cold surprise: my father would know exactly what kind of rope this is.
Then I was in the boat with a man's boot in my back and somebody was shouting at me to get down and stay down.
Eleven of us got off. Four did not.

We were maybe two hundred yards away when she went. It was not a great crash and roar the way it is in stories. She simply got lower, and then lower, and then the sea closed over the place where she had been. It went on doing what it had been doing all night, as though nothing had been taken out of the middle of it at all.
That is what frightened me most. Not the noise. The lack of it.
They put us ashore at Yarmouth and the town was kind to us, which happens more often than people expect.

The master found me on the second day. He was not angry. That was worse than if he had been. He asked me whose son I was and why I had come. I told him, and he listened. Then he said something I have carried for the rest of my life.
He said: "Young man, you ought to take this for a plain sign that you are not to be a seafaring man."
And then, because he was honest, he added: "Though I have said that to four lads and three of them are at sea now."
She simply got lower, and then lower.
York is four days' walk from Yarmouth. I had money enough for the road.

I have crossed oceans since. I have walked in country where the ground was on fire under a thin crust, and I have gone into the sea at night knowing what was in it. I want that understood before I say the next thing.
Four days' walk was the only journey I have ever found impossible.

I got as far as the road out of the town. I stood there with the milestone in front of me, and I could see the whole of it. The street. The door. The smell of tar coming out to meet me. And my father's face, doing the arithmetic of what my being there meant.
He would have taken me in. I knew that then and I know it now. He would not even have shouted.
That was exactly the trouble. I could have borne shouting.
I turned south instead, towards London, and I told myself it was only until I had something to show him.
I have noticed since that a man will cross an ocean to avoid a conversation.
London took my money in five weeks and gave me nothing back.

I copied letters for a scrivener near the Fleet. It is the only trade my father's ledgers ever got me. I slept in a room with four other men and a chimney that did not draw. In the mornings I went down to the pool and looked at the ships the way a hungry man looks in at a cookshop window.
I tried to sign aboard three of them.

The first master asked for my indenture papers. The second asked who I had sailed with. I said one voyage out of Hull that ended on the sand at Yarmouth. He laughed so hard he had to put his cup down.

The third did not ask anything. He looked at my hands, which were soft, and at my coat, which was too good. Then he said what they all meant: you are somebody's runaway son, and I am not taking that trouble aboard my ship.
Being right about a boy has never once stopped him.
A space the shape of a coffin, and no way out of it.
She was loading for the Guinea coast and she was to drop down river on the Tuesday tide.

I went aboard on the Monday night with a sack over my shoulder, up the plank behind two porters. Nobody looked at me twice. I was carrying something, and moving like a man who knew where he was going. I have since learned that this will get a person into almost anywhere.

I went down through the main hatch while they were still striking cargo below. I got in behind the water casks on the starboard side. There was a gap there between the casks and the ship's timbers, about as wide as my shoulders and about as long as I was tall.
I had bread, a bottle, a knife, a horn of tinder I could not use in a hold full of tar, and twenty feet of my father's rope.
My plan was simple, and I want to set it down honestly, because it was the plan of an idiot.

I would lie hidden two days. Then I would come up. We would be at sea, they could not put me ashore, and a ship is always short of hands. They would swear at me and put me to work and by Guinea I would be a sailor.
Every part of that was true except the timing, and the timing was the whole thing.
They battened the hatches on the Tuesday, in the rain, and I lay in the dark and listened to the ship come alive over my head.
I do not know how big a blow it was. From where I lay, all weather is the same weather. What I know is that on the second night the cargo began to work.

That is the word the sailors use, and it is a mild word for what it is. A ship's cargo is stowed tight. When it is not tight enough, the roll starts to move it, a finger's width at a time. And every roll makes the next roll easier.
I heard it start. A grinding, somewhere forward, that had not been there before.

I do not know what it was, even now. Bales, I think, and a tier of small casks on top of them. It came down across the mouth of my gap with a noise that went through the whole ship. When it stopped, the space I was lying in had no way out of it.
I put my hands out and felt along the whole of it, twice, on my knees in the black.
Timbers on one side. Casks on the other. A wall of something wedged and immovable at the end where I had come in.
And at the other end, a hole about the size of my chest, going away into the cargo.
I want to say that I was brave.

What I actually did was scream until my voice broke. Then I beat on the casks with the handle of my knife until my hand would not close. Then I lay down in a space the shape of a coffin and shook for what I am fairly sure was several hours.
Nobody came. Nobody could have come. There was a foot of oak and thirty tons of cargo between me and the men walking about over my head, and above all that there was a gale.
When I stopped, I was very calm, and the calm frightened me more than the screaming had.
Because in the calm I understood the arithmetic. Nobody was going to open that hatch until fine weather. Fine weather might be a week. My bottle held perhaps a pint.
Here is the thing I have never been able to explain to anyone who has not been in the dark.
It is not the dark that undoes you. It is that time stops.

You cannot tell an hour from four hours. You sleep and wake and have no idea which side of the sleep you are on. Twice I was certain that days had passed, and twice I later worked out that it had been a single night.
A man in that state stops being able to think, and then he stops being able to want to think, and after that he is finished, whatever water he has.
What saved me was the bell.
I heard it on the third or fourth time of waking: a small far sound coming down through the deck, and then, some while after, the same sound again.
A ship strikes her bell every half hour. Eight bells, and the watch changes, and it begins again at one.
I lay in the dark and counted bells.

I counted them for the rest of the time I was down there. When I slept I lost the count, and had to pick it up again from the next watch change. I marked the days by cutting the wood of the cask beside my head with the point of my knife.
My father counted his rope twice a day for thirty years. I had told him a boy could learn nothing from that but how to be bored.
In the hold of that ship I learned what he had actually been teaching. A man who has a number can hold on to it. A man with nothing to count comes apart.
I paid the rope out behind me as I went.
The water was the second problem and it was worse than the first.

I found it by knocking. A full cask and an empty cask do not answer the same. After some hours of crawling and knocking with my knuckles I had found four that answered full. They were all of them out beyond the hole at the end of my space.
Getting to them was where the rope came in.
I could not see. I could not leave a mark. A man who crawls twenty feet into a stack of cargo in absolute darkness and then turns around has no way on earth of knowing which turning brought him in.
So I made one end fast to the cask by my head, and paid the rope out behind me as I went. When I wanted to come back, I came back along it hand over hand.
Twenty feet of good hemp, well laid, tarred the winter before.
I had taken it out of my father's storehouse because I wanted to steal something and it was the thing nearest the door. That is the whole of the reason. There was no sense in it.
I have thought a great deal since about how little of my life I have arranged, and how much of it has been arranged for me.
The casks were oak and the bungs were driven home hard and set in the head, where I could not get at them.

I put the point of the knife into a stave, low down, and I turned it, and I kept turning it. It took — I do not know. Two watches. Three. The blade went in about a finger's depth and then would not go further. I sat back and cried a little. Then I went at it again from a different angle, and broke the plug of wood out sideways.
The water came out over my hand.
I have drunk better water since and I have never once enjoyed it as much.

Then I did the sensible thing, which surprised me: I whittled a peg and drove it into the hole. Because a cask that runs out into the bilge is worth nothing to anybody, and I had understood by then that I might be down there a long time.
There was salt beef in that hold too. I found a broached cask of it on the second crawl, and I lay with my hand on the meat and made myself put it back.
Salt meat and a pint of water a day is a way of dying that takes longer and hurts more.
I lived on ship's bread, which was in a cask I could reach and which I have loathed ever since.
They opened the hatch on the eleventh day.
I knew it was the eleventh because I had eleven marks on the cask beside my head. I have been proud of very few things in my life the way I am proud of those eleven marks.
Light came down through the cargo in a grey bar full of dust and it was the most violent thing I had ever seen. I had to put my arm over my eyes.
Then I shouted, and a man's voice above said, very slowly, "There is something down there."
They opened the hatch on the eleventh day.
The master was not kind, and I have never held it against him.
A stowaway is not a bold lad in a story. He is a man stealing a passage, eating stores that were counted out for a crew. And the ship will hang for it if she is short of water in the doldrums.
He put me on the pumps, and on the worst of the beef. He told me I would have no wage. And he told me that when we made a port, he would put me ashore in it, whatever port it was.
Then, that evening, he sent for me again.
He asked how I had got water.
I told him about the knocking, and the knife, and the peg.
He looked at me for a long moment and said, "Who taught you to plug it after?"
And I said, "Nobody. My father sold rope."
He did not understand that, and I did not explain it.

I went down into the dark of that hold a boy who thought his father was a frightened old man with a wall built out of bad luck. I came up out of it with eleven knife marks, a peg in a water cask, and twenty feet of stolen rope coiled on my arm.
I have never since called either of his two dull gifts dull.
We saw her a little after eight in the morning, hull down in the south-east, and for four hours she was simply a sail.

That is the part nobody puts in the stories. It is not a shout and a boarding. It is four hours of watching a triangle of white get slightly larger, and knowing, and having nothing whatever to do about it.
The master went up twice with the glass. The second time he came down he gave the order to make all sail, and after that no one on that deck pretended any more.
She was a rover out of Salé, and she was faster than us by about a third, and every man aboard could do that arithmetic without being told the numbers.
For four hours she was simply a sail.
I remember the last hour very clearly.

The carpenter sat down on the deck and took his shoes off and put them side by side, neatly, as though he were going to bed. I asked him why. He said a man swims better without them and that his father had drowned in his shoes.
The cook went below and came up with a knife I had never seen him use for cooking.
And I stood at the rail with my father's rope coiled on my arm. I had carried it everywhere since the hold and could not have said why. I thought about the milestone on the road out of Yarmouth.
Four days' walk. I could have been three years in York by then, in a bad temper, alive.
She came up on our quarter about two in the afternoon and put a shot across us, and when we did not strike, she put the next one into us.
I will not make a battle of it. It lasted less time than it takes to eat a meal.

They were sixty or seventy men and we were nineteen. They came over the rail in three places at once and they did it without shouting, which was somehow worse. Our mate went down in the first half minute. A man beside me put up his hands and was not hurt, and I saw that and put up mine.
I have wondered since whether I should be ashamed of how quickly I did it.
I have decided that I should not. There is a kind of courage that is only a slower way of getting men killed, and the mate had it, and he is at the bottom of the sea off the Canaries.
They took the ship, and they took us, and then they sorted us.

That is the word. Sorted. We stood on our own deck and a man walked down the line. He looked at us the way my father looked at a delivery of hemp: for what would be usable, and for what would have to be thrown out.
He took the carpenter, obviously. He took the two strongest hands.
He came to me and I was eighteen and soft-handed and no use to anybody, and I understood, standing there, that being of no use was the most dangerous thing I had ever been.
So I did the only thing I could think of.
I said, in the little Portuguese I had picked up on the Guinea coast, that I could write and keep accounts.
He looked at me for a while.
Then he said, in better Portuguese than mine, "Show me."
They brought up the ship's book. I sat down on a hatch cover on a captured deck with a dead man forty feet away and I ruled a line and set down a column of figures in my father's small square hand.
The rover's captain kept me for himself.

I learned later that this was luck of a kind that people spend their whole lives without. The men who were sorted the other way went to the galleys, and I never heard of any of them again, and I have never once let myself imagine it in detail.
We were nine days to Salé.
The river came up brown and slow between two towns, and the whole place stood with its back to the land and its face to the sea.

There were ships from everywhere along the quays. Dutch cloth going ashore. Sugar in barrels that leaked sweetness onto the stones. A crate of ostrich feathers had broken somewhere and there were feathers caught along the base of a wall, moving in the wind.
I stood in that boat with my hands tied in front of me. I looked at it all and I thought, with perfect clarity: this is a port like Hull is a port.
Men were arguing about the price of something. A boy was selling water out of a skin. A dog was asleep in a doorway with its legs out.
I do not know what I had expected. Something more like the end of the world, I suppose.

That is the first thing Salé taught me, and it took about ninety seconds: the places where the worst thing in your life happens to you are ordinary places, and they go on being ordinary while it happens.
I was not sold in the market.

The captain kept me, which meant I went straight from the boat to a house. The house had a courtyard with a lemon tree in it. I slept the first night in a store-room off that courtyard, on a mat, with the door barred from the outside.
In the morning a woman I never learned the name of gave me bread and oil, and looked at me for a moment with an expression I could not read at all, and went away.
Then a man came and put a hoe in my hands and took me out to the garden, and that was that.
I was property for two years.
I want to set down exactly what it was like, because people ask, and because most of what they imagine is wrong in both directions.
Nobody beat me. Not once. I was worth money and money is not improved by damage.
I was fed the same food the household ate, which was better than anything I had eaten in London.

And none of that is the point. I did not understand that it was not the point until about the third month. I was pulling weeds in a hot garden, and I stopped, and looked at my hands, and thought: if I were to die here this afternoon, the loss would be his.
Not my mother's. Not my father's. His.
I had been sold out of my own life into somebody's inventory. I was a number in a ledger, and I knew exactly what that felt like from the other side, because I had written the ledgers.
That is the thing they took, and it is the only thing they took, and it is everything.
It came out of their mouths with the wrong bones in it. Within a week it had worn down to two syllables that were nearly right and not quite. After a month that was simply what I was called.
I answered to it. Of course I answered to it. You answer to whatever gets you fed.
But I lay on my mat that night and thought about my father, and about Bremen, and about a name that went into an English mouth as Kreutznaer and came out of it, thirty years later, as Crusoe.
York had filed my father's name.
I remember thinking, with a kind of black satisfaction: well, at least now I know what he lost.
This is a port like Hull is a port.
The last thing I will say about that first month is about the sound.
It came before dawn, from the tower, and it went out over the flat roofs, and it was a man's voice, unaccompanied, holding notes longer than any voice at home would have held them.
I did not understand one word of it. For a long time I did not want to.

But it came five times a day, always, in every weather, and the whole city bent itself around it. The arguing stopped and started again. The shops shut and opened. The man in the next courtyard put down what he was carrying and went in.
After a few weeks I found that I no longer needed to guess the hour.
I would be in the garden with the hoe. It would begin. And I would think: so it is that time.
My father, on a cold roof in York, had told me that one day I might have to know where I was without being told.
He had meant the star. He had meant latitude and a hand held up against the sky.

It did not occur to me for a long time that the same trick works on time. I had begun to learn it in a garden I was not allowed to leave, from a voice I could not understand — saying words I would one day say myself.

ch.t: Chapter Five. The House and the Boat
p: Chapter Five. The House and the Boat
I learned Arabic the way a dog learns it.

Nobody sat me down. Nobody explained a single rule. Words came at me attached to things: to a hoe, to a bucket, to bring that here and not like that and are you deaf. I picked them up one at a time, badly, in the wrong order, with no idea which of them were polite.

For about four months I spoke like a rude child. Then one evening I said something in the courtyard and the woman who brought the bread laughed, and I understood why she was laughing, and that was the day I could speak.
The boy taught me most of it. His name was Xury.
I was property for two years.
He was perhaps thirteen and he had been in that house longer than I had, and he was quicker than me at everything except figures.

I have to be careful here, because of how these things get told. He was not my little servant. Nobody had given him to me. We were two pieces of the same man's property, and if the master had sold either of us the other would have had no more say in it than a chair has.
That is what we had in common, and it is a strange, strong thing to have in common.

He taught me the words. I taught him to write his name, in the dust of the courtyard, with a stick. He made me do it about forty times and then he could do it, and he sat looking at it for a while, and then he rubbed it out with his foot before anybody came.
I did not ask why. I knew why.
My master's business was the sea, and after the first year he found out I was useful on it.
He kept a boat, a good one, with a little cabin forward and a lateen sail. He went out in her to fish, which is what men of means did there on a fine morning, the way men here go out with a gun.
I was sent along to work her. Xury was sent along to do everything else.
And I found out something that surprised me very much, which is that I was good at it.

I had the wind, and the way the boat sat, and the shape of the swell. I do not know where any of it came from, unless it came from eighteen years of standing on a quay watching — which I had always thought was time wasted.

By the second summer my master would sit in the stern with his line and let me sail her. Once he said to a friend of his, in Arabic, thinking I did not have enough of it yet: this one has the sea in his hands.
I have never in my life been so pleased and so sick at the same time.
I should say something about the sound now, because two years is long enough for a sound to stop being strange.
It went on being five times a day. That does not change.

By the second year I knew the words, though nobody had taught them to me either, and I knew what they meant, though I would have denied being interested. I knew that the first one before dawn was the hardest and that a man who came out for it in the winter dark was doing something difficult.
I saw my master do it in a wet garden when he had a fever, and be short with everybody afterwards, and do it again the next morning.
I want to be exact about my state of mind, because it would be very easy to make this tidier than it was.
I did not believe. I did not want to believe. I was a slave in that house and I was not going to be talked into loving the thing that held me.

But I had grown up in a country where a man's religion was a coat he put on for an hour on Sunday. Here was a thing that cut the day into pieces and would not let anybody alone. I could not make myself despise it.
I filed it away. I told myself I would think about it when I was free.
I did think about it when I was free. It took me eleven more years and an island.
I taught him to write his name in the dust of the courtyard.
The chance came in the third spring, and it came because my master was too comfortable.

He was to take out two guests, and he had us provision the boat the night before, and in the morning he did not come. He sent word that we were to go out and fish for the house instead. One of his men would come to keep an eye on the pair of us: a grown man of his household, who was no sailor at all.
So there were three of us in the boat and one of them could not swim.

I had two years of that coast in my head by then. I knew the current. I knew where the wind went in the afternoon. I knew that nobody would think anything was wrong until nightfall, and that nobody would come out looking in the dark.
I had put a great deal of bread aboard the night before, and a jar of water more than we needed. I had told Xury nothing. A boy of thirteen cannot keep a secret in his face for twelve hours.
I did it about two hours out, with the shore a low brown line.
I want to set down what I actually did, without making it braver or better than it was.

I looked at the distance first. I made myself count: the swell, the set of the current, how far a man could swim with the sun where it was. I have wondered since whether that counting was mercy or bookkeeping. Perhaps at eighteen there is no difference.
Then I took him round the waist and put him over the side.

He came up shouting. I told him, in his own language, which I had learned in his own house, that the shore was there and he could reach it easily. I told him I had no wish to hurt him. And I told him that if he tried to come back over the gunwale, I would not be able to promise him anything.
He swore at me. Then he turned and swam.
I watched him until I was sure. He was going strongly. The last I saw of him he was standing up in the shallows about a mile off, still shouting things I could hear only as a noise.
I have thought about him a great deal more than he has probably thought about me.
This one has the sea in his hands.
Xury had not moved the whole time.
When I came back to the tiller he looked at me and said, very carefully, "Where are we going?"
He said, "South is nothing. South is a hundred days of nothing."
"Then we go until we find something."
He was quiet for a while. Then he said the sentence I have carried longer than almost anything anybody has ever said to me. He said:
"If they take us, they will not sell me. Do you understand? They will not sell me. They will make an example."
I did understand. That was the terrible part. I had a country somewhere, and a name in a ledger in York, and if the worst came I was a runaway who could be sold again.
He had none of that. What he was risking and what I was risking were not the same size at all, and he knew it exactly, and he came anyway.
Then he took the water jar and stowed it properly under the thwart, where it would not go over if we had weather.

We ran south with the land on our left hand until the light went. Then we ran south by the star my father had shown me on a cold roof in York. It stood lower in that sky than it had ever stood at home.
I remember thinking that he would have liked to know it worked.

ch.t: Chapter Six. What I Would Not Sell
p: Chapter Six. What I Would Not Sell
Freedom, for the first eleven days, was mostly about water.

We went south with the land on our left hand and we did not dare go ashore. For the first week we were still in country where a boat like ours would be known, and a boy like Xury would be worth money to whoever brought him back.
So we drank a little and we were thirsty all day and we drank a little more.
I had done a calculation on the second morning and I did not tell him the answer.

That is one of the small ugly parts of being the older one. I knew we had nine days of water at what we were drinking. I knew that nine days south would put us nowhere in particular. And I sat at the tiller with that in my head and said pleasant things about the weather.
We lay in the bottom of the boat with the sail over us.
We went ashore on the twelfth day because we had to.
I ran her into a creek mouth at dusk, and we sat in the boat in the dark with the jar empty and listened to the country.

It was not quiet. That is what nobody tells you. There were things calling all night in three or four different voices, and once something big went into the water somewhere upstream, and the noise it made going in was not the noise a small thing makes.
Xury did not sleep. Neither did I. We lay in the bottom of the boat with the sail over us like two children hiding from a thunderstorm, which is exactly what we were.
At first light we found the stream, and it was sweet, and we filled everything we had.
And while we were filling the last jar, the thing on the bank stood up.
I had the master's gun. I had loaded it perhaps six times in my life.
It was a big cat. I never learned what kind and I have deliberately never looked it up, because in my memory it is the size of a pony and I would rather keep it that way.

It was about forty feet off, up on the bank above us, and it was not crouching or snarling or any of the things that would have been useful. It was standing quite still with its head down, working out whether we were worth the walk.
Xury said, very quietly, "Do not run."

I want that recorded. I was twenty-one years old and had crossed an ocean. The piece of advice that saved my life on that riverbank came from a thirteen-year-old. He had never been more than a mile from Salé until eleven days before.
I did not run. I put the gun up and I waited until it took two steps, and then I fired.
I hit it somewhere that mattered. It went down and got up and went sideways into the bushes, and we heard it going away up the slope for a long time, and then we heard it stop.
We found it an hour later, dead, about two hundred yards off. I have no pride at all in the shot. I have some in the fact that neither of us ran.
People came out of the trees that afternoon to look at us.
There were perhaps a dozen, and they stood off at a distance and looked, and we stood by the boat and looked back, and this went on for a long time.
Then Xury did the sensible thing, which I would not have thought of.

He walked ten steps away from the boat and put down the gun and the knife where they could see him do it. Then he walked back, pointed up the slope towards the dead animal, and made a wide gesture: it is there, and it is yours.

They understood. Of course they understood. They had been watching us since dawn and they knew perfectly well what had happened, and I think they had been waiting to see whether we would be stupid about it.

They took the skin and most of the meat. In the evening two of them came down with a clay pot of something cooked and a bundle of dried fish, and stood while we ate some of it. I understood later that this was courtesy, and also good sense.
They were not simple people. They were people with a river, a village, and no particular reason to trust two strangers with a gun.
We stayed three days. I have often thought that if the ship had not come we might have stayed for good, and that it would not have been the worst life.
It was standing quite still, working out whether we were worth the walk.
The Portuguese ship came up the coast on the fourth morning.
I put out and stood across her bows with the sail flat and my shirt on an oar. She backed her topsail and let us come alongside. A rope came down, and that was the end of the running.
The captain was a small grey man from Lisbon who had been forty years at sea. He fed us. He would not take the boat as payment, though it was worth something and I offered it twice.

He said a thing I have repeated to a great many people since. He said that he had once been picked up out of the water himself, and that the man who did it took nothing. He had been paying that debt to strangers for thirty years, and expected to die still owing on it.
Then, on the fourth evening out, over the remains of his dinner, he made me an offer for Xury.
He did it kindly. That is important. He was not a slaver and there was nothing in his face but ordinary business.
He said that the boy was quick, that he would train him, and he named a sum — a good sum, a sum that would have set me up in Brazil with land instead of debt.
And he added, because he was a decent man by the standards of his trade, that he would set him free in ten years.
He was surprised. He asked me why, and I found that I could not answer him for a moment, and then I said:
"Because eleven days ago I was worth about the same, and somebody was making that arithmetic about me."
He looked at me for a while.
Then he said, "You will be poor in Brazil."

And he said, "Well," and poured more wine, and never raised it again. In the morning he offered Xury a place aboard as a paid boy, at a real wage. He did not have to do that. I have thought about it every time anyone has told me the world is simply cruel.
Xury took it. He was right to take it.

He stayed with that ship four years and I did not see him again for a long time. When I did, he was a grown man with a mate's certificate and a scar on his hand. He had a great deal to say about my seamanship, none of it flattering.
But that is later, and it belongs to another part of this.
"Because eleven days ago I was worth about the same."
We came into Brazil in the spring, and I went up the country with almost nothing.
Here is the thing I want to be honest about, because it is the whole point of everything that comes after, and if I dress it up the rest will make no sense.
I had refused good money for a human being, and I knew that most men in that harbour would not have refused it, and I carried that around inside me like a warm coal for years.
I was so pleased about the large thing I had got right that I never once looked at the small thing I had got wrong.
My father had asked me for one sentence. I had given him my word, and broken it, and let him stand on the end of a pier and watch a ship take his last son away.
I had crossed an ocean and refused a fortune and I had never written him a letter.

There is a kind of man who will do the noble thing in front of witnesses and cannot do the plain thing in private. I was twenty-two years old, and I was exactly that man. It was going to cost me twenty-eight years of my life.

ch.t: Chapter Seven. Brazil, and the First of September
p: Chapter Seven. Brazil, and the First of September
Four years in Brazil made me a farmer, which is the last thing anybody would have expected, including me.

I bought poor land because it was what I could afford, and I planted tobacco because it was what the poor land would take. For the first two years I ate rice and worked until dark. I owed money to a man in the town who was patient with me for reasons I never understood.
The third year the crop was good. The fourth year it was better.
By the fifth I had a house with a floor in it, two men working with me for wages, and a neighbour on either side.
I was twenty-six, and solvent, and about as far from the sea as a man can get while still being able to smell it.
I have gone over that year many times, and I cannot find the moment where it went wrong, because nothing went wrong. That is the difficulty. Everything was fine, and I ruined it anyway.
About as far from the sea as a man can get while still being able to smell it.
My neighbours came to me in the winter with a proposition.

They had done their arithmetic. Field hands were dear in Brazil because the trade was licensed and the licence-holders took their cut. But a ship going quietly down to the Guinea coast, fitted out by three or four planters between them, could bring people back for their own estates and pay nothing to anybody.
They wanted my share of the money and they wanted me aboard, because I knew that coast, and had a little Arabic, and had been down there twice.

They put it to me across my own table, over my own wine, and they were not wicked men. That is the thing I have never been able to make anyone understand. They were my neighbours. One of them had sat up two nights with me when I had the fever. They spoke about it the way men speak about buying oxen, and they meant no harm by it, and they would have been genuinely puzzled to be told there was any harm in it to mean.
I said it plainly and I did not soften it, and one of them was angry and one of them laughed, and the third looked at me afterwards in a way I did not like at all.
I have never once regretted that no.
But here is what happened next, and it is the reason I am writing any of this down.
Two months later a different offer came. A ship going up the coast for hides and dye-wood and whatever else was going. Ordinary cargo. Ordinary trade. No people in the hold.
They wanted a supercargo who could keep the books.

Why? I have had a great deal of time to answer that, and the honest answer is small and shabby. My tobacco was doing well and it was doing well slowly. The voyage would make in five months what my fields would make in three years.

And under that, further down where I did not look at it: I was bored. I was twenty-six and I had a house with a floor and two men working for wages, and every morning was the same morning, and somewhere out past the river mouth there were ships going somewhere.
The same want that walked me down to Hull at eighteen was sitting in my chest at twenty-six with its boots off, perfectly comfortable, waiting.
I want to put the two things side by side, because for years I refused to.
I had turned down a fortune rather than buy a human being, and I was proud of it, and I was right to be.

Then I signed for a cargo of hides because I was restless. I left my fields to a manager. I did not tell my mother I was going, and I did not write to my father. He had not had a letter from me in eight years. He was, though I did not know it, already dead.
A man can be very brave about the enormous thing and never once do the small dull one.
The small dull one, in my case, was: stay where you are and write a letter.
We sailed on the first of September, in the year 1659.
I did not notice the date until we were three days out and I was writing up the book. Then I sat looking at the figures for a while.
The first of September, 1651, I had gone down the Humber with my father's rope on my arm.

I am not a superstitious man. I have never believed the sea keeps accounts. But I will say that I did not like it, and that I did not write it in the book, and that I have never since been able to see that date without something turning over in me.
She hit a bar with the whole weight of herself and stopped dead.
The storm took us on the twelfth day and it did not let go for eleven.

It drove us west and then north-west, out of any water we knew, past the point where the master could tell me within two hundred miles where we were. We lost the mainmast on the fourth day and a man with it. We lost the boat on the sixth. After that we were simply a thing being pushed.
On the eleventh morning a man at the head shouted the word every one of us had been waiting eleven days to hear and dreading equally.
Then, almost at once, we struck.

She hit a bar with the whole weight of herself and stopped dead, and the sea began to break clean over her, and I understood in about four seconds that the ship was finished and that we had perhaps an hour.
We got the small boat over. Eleven of us in it.

I do not remember getting in. I remember that I had gone below one last time and come up with almost nothing sensible. No water. No bread. What I had done, without thinking about it at all, was take my father's rope off the peg where I kept it and put it over my head and one shoulder.
Twenty feet of good hemp, well laid, eight years old and still sound.
Then we were in the boat and away, and the sea took us the way a hand sweeps crumbs off a table.
A wave came in behind us that I did not see, and I have always been glad I did not see it.

The boat was simply gone. There was no capsizing, no shouting, nothing you could describe as an event. One moment there were eleven men in a boat and the next there was water, and I was under it, and being rolled along the bottom hard enough that I have marks on my back to this day.
I came up and got one breath.
The next one took me in again, and this time it carried me a long way, and when it put me down my knees hit sand.

I got up and ran. The next one caught me at the shoulders, knocked me flat and dragged me back. I got up and ran again. I did that four times. The fourth time I got up, the water only came to my ankles. I went twenty steps further and lay down on the wet sand and could not move at all.
The first night of twenty-eight years.
I lay there a long while. Then it got dark, and I made myself get up, because of the tide and because of whatever might live there.
There was fresh water in a hollow half a mile inland and I drank until I was sick.

Then I climbed a tree, because I could think of nothing else to do, and I wedged myself in a fork with my father's rope round the trunk and round my waist and knotted, so that I would not fall out when I slept.
That is the first thing that rope did for me on that island. It was not the last.
I hung in the dark and listened to the sea taking my ship apart three hundred yards away, and I did the only arithmetic that was left to do.
Eleven men had gone into the boat.
I could see the whole beach in the moonlight, both ways, and there was nothing on it but weed.
I want to write down exactly what I said out loud, because I have never forgotten it and because it was not a prayer, whatever it sounds like.
I said: "There is nobody left to blame but me."
And then I slept, hanging in a tree, on the first night of twenty-eight years.

ch.t: Chapter Eight. What the Sea Gave Back
p: Chapter Eight. What the Sea Gave Back
In the morning the ship was still there.
The tide had gone out and left her sitting on the bar with a list on her, about a mile off, whole enough that I could see the stump of the mainmast and a rag of canvas moving.
I sat on the sand and looked at her for a long time, and I felt something I am not proud of, which was fury.
If we had stayed aboard, all eleven of us would have walked off her dry at low water.

Every man in that boat was dead because we had been frightened at the wrong hour. I have seen men decide well and die anyway, since. But that morning I sat on a beach and understood that fear is not a warning. Fear is a noise, and sometimes it is a noise about nothing, and it had just drowned ten men.
Then I stopped thinking about it, because the tide turns twice a day and there is only so much daylight.
I made twelve trips over the next eleven days.
I will not pretend it was brave. It was a mile of flat water and I was twenty-seven and I had nothing else to do that day.
Getting up her side was the hard part, and it was the rope that did it — I threw the coil until a fluke of the broken forechains caught it, and went up hand over hand with my feet on the planking.
Then I stood on the deck of a dead ship with the water sloshing about below and I began, God forgive me, to feel almost cheerful.
I made twelve trips over the next eleven days.
The first day I built a raft out of spare topmasts and planks, lashed with — well, with everything that would lash, and I want to be exact here, because people always ask about the rope.
My father's twenty feet were not enough to build a raft. Of course they were not. There were coils of proper cordage in that ship, hundreds of fathoms of it, and that is what the raft was built with.
What the twenty feet did was get me aboard the first time.
I have thought a great deal about how the small thing you happen to be carrying decides whether you ever reach the big thing you need.
I will not write out a list of what I took. Lists are the death of a story and I have read books that were nothing else.
But there were four things that mattered, and I will name them.
The carpenter's chest, which was worth more than everything else together and which I nearly left behind on the second trip because it was heavy.

Two guns, a fowling piece, and all the powder — the powder in three lots, kept in three places afterwards, because a man with all his powder in one cave is one lightning strike from being an animal again.
Bread, rice, three cheeses, five pieces of dried goat, and a little grain that I thought was worthless and was not.
And a small chest of tools and instruments out of the master's cabin. There was a quadrant in it, broken. Two knives. A pair of scissors. Pens, ink dried in the pot, and paper.
I sat on the sand that evening with the paper in my hands.
Nobody was ever going to read it. I knew that quite clearly by then.
I kept it anyway, and it is why you are reading this at all, so make of that what you like.
On the thirteenth day the wind came round to the north-east and blew hard for two nights, and in the morning the bar was empty.
She had gone in the dark, without a sound I could hear over the surf, in the same quiet way the ship in Yarmouth Roads had gone eight years before.
I stood on the beach and looked at the empty place.

I had everything off her that a man could get, and I still stood there for the better part of an hour. When I walked away I understood what I had just watched: the last piece of the world I came from going under water.
In the morning the bar was empty.
It took me nine days to learn that I was on an island.

I climbed the hill in the middle on the fourth day and I could see water on three sides, and I told myself the fourth side might go on for ever, and I spent five more days walking until I proved that it did not.
I sat down when I proved it. That is the honest word for what I did. My legs stopped holding me up and I sat down in the grass.
Eleven miles long. Perhaps five across at the wide end. Goats on the high ground. Birds. No people, no smoke, no path.
I made myself say it out loud, because a thing said out loud can be worked with and a thing kept in the chest cannot:
"I am the only man on this island, and there is no ship, and nobody is coming."
Then I got up and walked back to my tent, because it was going to rain.
I found the grave in the eleventh week.

I was cutting up towards the high ground after goats, along the top of a small valley on the north side where a stream came down. I came out onto a flat shelf of grass above the water. It was the best place on the whole island to put a house, which is what made me stop.
There was a low heap of stones on it. Man-high, and half again as long. Too neat for weather to have made.
I stood looking at it for a while with my heart going.
At the head of it, set upright and wedged with smaller stones, there was a flat slab about the size of a book, and there was writing cut into it.
I got down on my knees in the wet grass and turned my head sideways, because the light was low and coming from the wrong side.
I want to be very careful with what I say next, because it is the hinge of my whole life and I have seen people make it sentimental.

I could read it because for two years I had been the property of a man in Salé. I had learned his language out of the mouths of the people who owned me. I had been taught my letters by a boy of thirteen, who rubbed his own name out of the dust with his foot so that nobody would see.
I had spent eight years thinking of those two years as the hole in the middle of my life. The thing that had been taken from me. The part I would not talk about.

And then I knelt on a shelf of grass on an island with no name, four thousand miles from that garden, in front of a heap of stones. And it turned out that the only thing in my whole life that let me understand what was written there was the worst thing that had ever happened to me.
I sat back on my heels and I laughed, and then I did not laugh.
The writing was Arabic. I could read it.
It said a name: Yusuf ibn Abdullah.
It said, under the name, the plainest sentence a man can cut into rock, and I will give it here in English as near as I can put it: he came from the sea, and he was alone, and here he is buried.
And under that there was a date.

It was written in the numerals I had learned in Salé, and I could read every figure of it perfectly well, and it meant nothing to me at all — because it was not counted from the year I counted from. It was a year in the other reckoning, the one my master's household used, and I had never once bothered to learn how the two lined up.
I sat with my hand flat on that stone until it got dark.
Somebody had carved it. That was the thing I could not get past.
A man cannot cut his own headstone and then lie down under a heap of stones and pull them over himself. Somebody had done it for him.
And whoever the second one was, he had cut the letters, and laid the stones, and then walked away down this same valley — and there was nothing else on this island. No hut. No wall. No ashes.
Which meant that either he had got off, somehow, from an island that nobody comes to.
Or he had not, and I had simply not found him yet.

ch.t: Chapter Nine. The Star and the Bread
p: Chapter Nine. The Star and the Bread
The fever came in the second summer and it very nearly finished me.
It began with cold, which is an absurd thing to feel in that country. I sat by a fire in the middle of the afternoon in a shirt and two goatskins and shook until my teeth hurt.
Then the heat came, and after the heat, nothing much for a day and a half.
I have no clear memory of most of it. What I remember is one afternoon of it, and I remember that afternoon better than I remember whole years.
I could not cross four feet.
I woke on my side. I could see the water jar. It was about four feet from my hand.

I understood the whole of my situation in about the time it takes to read this sentence. If I could not cross four feet, I was going to die of thirst inside a hut, with water in the room, on an island with fruit and goats and a stream, because there was nobody to push a jar six inches.
Not the sea. Not the cannibals I had not yet heard of. Six inches.
I got to the jar in the end. It took a long time and I will not describe it.
But I lay there afterwards with the water going down my chin and I said something out loud, and it was the first honest thing I had said in eleven years.
I said, "I cannot do this by myself."
I want to stop here and be careful, because this is the part of the account where a man is expected to tell you that the heavens opened.

I got better over about nine days. I ate. I mended the hut where the rain had come in. And the sentence I had said sat there in the middle of my head like a stone in a boot, and would not be walked off.
Because I had known it was true for a long time and had never said it.

Everything I had was luck. The ship on the bar. The rope that caught the chains. The grain I thought was rubbish. Ten men in a boat and one on a beach, and the one on the beach was not the strongest or the best.
I had spent eleven years congratulating myself on being ingenious.
Sitting there mending a roof, I could not any longer make the accounts balance. There was too much on the credit side that I had not put there.

I am not going to write out how I got from that to what I did next. It took four months, and most of it happened in my hands rather than my head — while I was walking, while I was mending nets, while I was lying awake.

I will only say this. I had lived two years in a house where a man went out into a wet garden with a fever because it was the hour. At the time I told myself I was watching a prisoner's routine. I had been wrong. I had been watching a free man.
And I will say that the first time I tried it, I knelt down on the sand and got as far as putting my hands on my knees and then stopped, because I had realised something ridiculous.
I did not know which way to face.
Here is what I actually knew.
Mecca lies a long way east of Salé, and somewhat south. I knew that because in that house you cannot help knowing it — the whole building was arranged around it.
I knew I was a very long way west of Salé, and I knew, from the wreck's reckoning before the storm, roughly how far south.
What I did not know was where I was now, and how much of the world lay between.
I sat on the sand and laughed at myself, and then I went and got the broken quadrant out of the chest.
It was broken. Of course it was broken. It had been broken for eleven years and I had kept it because I keep everything.
Which is when I remembered the shelf of grass.
It took me two days to find what I was looking for, and I found it about sixty paces from the heap of stones, under an overhang where the rock came out over the stream.
Somebody had lived there. Not built — lived. There was a flat place worn in the floor. There was a ring of stones black on the inside. There was a fish-hook made out of a nail.

And in a fold of rock at the back there was something wrapped in the rotted remains of what had once been cloth. It was a disc of brass about the size of my palm, green all over, with a ring at the top and marks around the rim.
An astrolabe. A small one, a seaman's, worn thin at the edge.
I sat down in another man's house and held it in both hands.
He had come from the sea and been alone. He had this in his pocket when he came. He had used it, presumably, exactly as I was about to use it, and for the same purpose.
And then he had died, and somebody had cut his name in a stone.
I said, out loud, to nobody: "Right. Then you can help me."
A disc of brass about the size of my palm, green all over.
It took the whole of that winter.
I cleaned the brass with sand and wet ash. Half the scale was eaten away and I re-cut the missing part by eye, which sounds impossible and is merely slow.

I took the altitude of the sun at noon on nine clear days and averaged them, because my hands shake and one measurement is a guess. I took the star my father had shown me on a roof in York, and it stood so low over the sea that I had to go up the hill to see it clear of the haze.
I got my latitude. I am fairly confident of it to this day.

Longitude I could not get. Nobody could, then. What I had instead was the ship's dead reckoning up to the eleventh day of the storm, and eleven days of being pushed by a wind whose direction I remembered, and a great deal of arithmetic.
I set it down in columns, in my father's small square hand, on paper I had carried off a wreck.
And at the end of it I had a direction: a little north of east, and I could put a figure on it, and the figure was probably wrong by ten degrees and possibly by thirty.
I have been asked, since, whether that troubled me. Whether it was worth doing at all, if I could not be sure.
It did trouble me. For about a week.

Then I worked out the only answer there is. A man who cannot know is not thereby excused from trying. The trying is done with what he actually has. And if he has done the arithmetic honestly, then the arithmetic is what he owes.
I drove two posts into the sand outside my door, lined up on my figure, so that I would not have to do it again every morning in the dark.
The calendar was harder, and I solved it worse.

I had my post with the notches. I knew exactly how many days I had been on that island — I had cut every one of them, and missed only about a fortnight during the fever, which I later corrected as best I could.
What I did not have was the other reckoning. The one on the stone. The one the year in Salé had been counted in.
I knew it went by the moon. I knew a month began when the new moon was seen. I did not know what month it was, and there was nobody within a thousand miles to tell me, and no book.
So I did the only thing available.

I began keeping months by the moon, from the first new moon after I decided, and I numbered them. I chose one and kept it as the month of the fast. And I wrote down plainly, on the paper, that I had chosen it and how — so that if I was ever again among people, I could be told how wrong I had been.
I was probably wrong. I have never found out by how much.
I kept it for sixteen years.
I will pass over the farming quickly, because Defoe's kind of book would give you forty pages of it and I would rather cut off a finger.

The grain I thought was rubbish came up in the wet corner where I had shaken out a bag. It took four harvests before I had enough to eat any of it, because for three years I ate none and planted all of it, which was the hardest thing I did on that island, harder than the fever.
I made bread in the eleventh year. It was bad bread.

I made pots. It took me two years to make a pot that would hold water, and about two hundred that would not, and when I finally lifted a whole one out of the fire I sat down on the ground and could not speak.

I got goats. I built a fence badly, and then a better one, and eventually I had milk, and after milk, butter, and I do not think any king in Europe was ever as pleased with anything as I was with butter.
Two posts in the sand, so that I would not have to do it again in the dark.

By the fifteenth year I had a house dug into a bank, a fenced field, a herd, and a boat I had made and could not launch. I had two posts in the sand outside my door. And I had a headstone up the valley that I visited perhaps four times a year and swept with my hand.
I want to record something here that will sound like a lie.
Not resigned. Not making the best of it. Happy, in a plain daily way that I had never once been in York or London or Brazil, where I had always been on my way to something.
I had food I had grown, a roof I had cut, an hour I could tell without being told, and a direction I had worked out myself with a dead man's brass.
I used to think about the boy standing at the rail with salt drying on his face, deciding his father was a frightened old man who had built a wall out of bad luck.
I would have liked ten minutes with him. I would not have wasted them on advice. I would just have shown him the butter.
In the sixteenth I went down to the shore on an ordinary morning to look at my boat, and there was a print of a man's naked foot in the sand.
That is what I want you to understand before anything else. Not a trail. Not a line of them coming up out of the water and going away into the trees, which would have been a fact I could follow.
One naked human foot, pressed into wet sand, above the last tide line.
I stood over it for a long time.
Then I went twenty paces one way and twenty the other, and there was nothing. I went down to the water and back. I went up into the dry sand where nothing holds a mark. Nothing.

A man does not arrive at a beach, put down one foot, and vanish. Which meant the rest had been taken by the tide, and that meant it was recent, and that meant somebody had been standing exactly there, on my island, within about six hours.
One naked human foot, pressed into wet sand.
I do not remember getting home.

I have a clear memory of standing over the print, and then a clear memory of being inside my own door with the ladder pulled up after me and my heart going so hard I could feel it in my teeth, and almost nothing in between. I am told this happens to soldiers.
I stayed in for three days.
Three days, on no food to speak of, listening. I did not light a fire. I did not go out to the goats, and they suffered for it, and I lay in the dark hearing them and did not go.

I have been frightened perhaps six times in my life in a way that stopped me thinking. In the hold of that ship. Twice in the storm. On the bank of that river with the cat. And three days in my own house because of a hole in some sand.
On the fourth day I made myself go back, and I made myself do the one thing I had been avoiding, which was to measure it.

I had told myself a story by then. A good one. I had gone down to that beach some weeks before to look at the boat, and I had been barefoot, and it was my own print, and I was an old man on his own who had frightened himself with his own foot.
I lay down beside it and put my foot into it.
It was longer than mine by the breadth of two fingers, and wider, and the toes had spread in a way mine never have because I have worn shoes since I was three.
I lay there in the sand with my leg out and I understood that the story was not true.
It was longer than mine by the breadth of two fingers.
Here is the thing I have never been able to explain to anybody who has not lived alone.
For fifteen years I had wanted a sail. Every single day. I had climbed the hill and looked, in all weathers, for fifteen years, at an empty sea.

And the first proof I ever had that another human being existed within a thousand miles of me — one footprint, no threat, no violence, nothing but the plain fact of another man — sent me into a hole in the ground for three days.
I have thought about it for the rest of my life and this is the best I can do.
I did not want people. I wanted rescue.

Rescue is a thing that happens to you on your own terms, at your own convenience, on a ship with a captain who feeds you. What I had found on that beach was not rescue. It was somebody else's will, loose on my island, doing what it liked.
I had been the only fact in that place for fifteen years. Now I was not. And it turned out that a great deal of what I had been calling contentment had been resting quietly on being alone in charge.
That was not a comfortable thing to learn at forty-three.
I became, over the next two years, a very strange animal.
I moved the goats inland and split the herd in three, so that no one place would show a man that there was a herd at all.
I stopped burning fires by day. I cooked at night, under the overhang, where the smoke broke up in the rock before it got out.
I planted my grain in five small patches instead of one field, in among the scrub, where they looked like nothing.
I made a second entrance to my house that came out in a thicket, and I kept a ladder there, and I never once used it for eleven years and never once stopped keeping it ready.
And I walked everywhere on stone and shingle. Two years of walking the long way round, over rock, so as not to put my own foot into sand.
Fifteen years I had lived openly on that island like a man in his own kitchen. After the print, I lived in it like a mouse.
This was a place they came to, and went away from.
I found the rest of it in the third year, at the far end, on a beach on the south-west side that I had been to perhaps twice in eighteen years because there is nothing there.
There was a place where fires had been made.

There were bones. Human ones. I am not going to describe them and I am not going to pretend I stood there and reasoned calmly about the customs of other nations, because I did not. I went about forty yards up the beach and was violently sick, and then I sat down on a rock with my back to it.

They came from somewhere else. That was the first thing I made myself work out, sitting on that rock. This was not a village. Nobody lived here. This was a place they came to, in boats, from another shore, and did what they did, and went away.
Which meant they would come again.
And it meant that for eighteen years, while I was building fences and being pleased about butter, boats had been landing at the other end of my island, and I had never known.
They came three more times in six years, and I watched all three from the hill with my heart going, and I did nothing.
I had worked it out on paper, the way I work everything out. I had four guns and one pair of hands. I could kill perhaps five of them before they reached me, and there were never fewer than twenty.
But that was not really why.
The real reason took me two years to say plainly to myself, and it was this: they had never once done me any harm, and had never once come looking for me, and I was not the magistrate of that ocean.

I hated what they did on that beach. I hate it now. But I noticed, sitting on my hill with a gun across my knees, how badly I wanted a reason to go down there — and how much of that wanting was eighteen years of having nobody to be angry at.
A man alone becomes very good at dressing up what he wants as what is right.
I do not remember standing up.
The twenty-fourth year. March, by my post.
There were two boats and about thirty men, and they had three prisoners with them, and I was up on the hill lying flat in the grass with the glass.
They killed one almost at once.
He came straight up the beach and into the trees on my side of the island, running the way a man runs when running is the last thing he has, and three of them came after him.

He was faster than they were. He was much faster. He had about four hundred yards on them by the time he reached the creek, and he went into it and across without slowing and came up the near bank into the scrub, and that is where I was.
I had perhaps ten seconds to decide.
I would like to tell you that I weighed it. I did not weigh anything. I came out of the scrub between him and the three of them with a gun in each hand and I do not remember standing up.

I killed one. The second I hit with the barrel of the empty gun. The third stopped dead about fifteen paces off, looked at me for one long moment, and turned and ran back the way he had come — and he must have told them something, because the boats went before dark and did not come back to that island for eleven years.
The man I had pulled out of it was on the ground behind me, and when I turned round he did something I have never been able to get out of my head.
He came up on his knees, and took my foot, and put it on his own head.
I knew exactly what it meant. Anybody would.
And I want to write down honestly what happened inside me in the two or three seconds while my foot was on that man's head, because if I leave it out the rest is worthless.
For about two seconds, I liked it.
Twenty-four years alone. Not one voice. And here was a living man on his knees telling me, in the oldest language there is, that I was the master and he was the thing.
Then I remembered a hot garden in Salé, and a boy of thirteen writing his own name in the dust with a stick and rubbing it out with his foot before anybody came.
I took my foot off his head so fast I nearly fell over.

I got him up. He did not understand why. He tried twice more over the next two days to do it again and I stopped him both times, and the second time I was angry, and he could not think what he had done wrong.
That took months to undo. Longer than teaching him English.
I have thought since that the cruellest thing about what had been done to that man, and to me, and to Xury, is how quickly it teaches the person it is done to that it is normal.
I took my foot off his head so fast I nearly fell over.
He was, I would guess, about twenty-six. He had a healed break in his left forearm that had set crooked. He could run further than any man I have ever met.
And within a month it was perfectly clear which of us was the ignorant one.

I had been eating a small blue crab for years that he would not let me touch after the rains. I had never worked out why the stream by the north valley ran low in some dry seasons and not others; he found the seep in one afternoon by looking at where two kinds of grass met. He could tell me at dawn whether it would be worth going out in the boat, from the birds, and he was right about four times in five, and I was right about half the time after twenty-four years.
He made me a fishing line in an evening that was better than anything I had made in two decades.

I taught him English, and to read it. I taught him figures. And on a clear night I took him up the hill and showed him the star that does not move, and how to hold a hand up to it, and how the whole of the sky turns round that one point and that point alone.
He liked that better than anything else I ever showed him.
I did it on the first day, because it was a Friday by my post, and because I had to call him something, and because — let me be exact — it did not occur to me for one second to ask.
I asked him in the fifth month.

He told me. It was three sounds and I got the first one wrong twice and the second one wrong three times, and he laughed at me, which was the first time I ever heard him laugh, and he said it slowly four times until I had it.
And I stood there with his name finally in my mouth and thought about Bremen.

My father's name went into English mouths as Kreutznaer and came out of them, worn down, as Crusoe. My own name went into a house in Salé and came out two syllables shorter, and I lay on a mat and thought bitterly about what had been taken.
And then I had done exactly the same thing to another man inside about ninety seconds of meeting him, and had not noticed, and would never have noticed if I had not thought to ask.
I have set him down in these pages as Friday all the same.

I thought about it for a long time before I decided. But this is meant to be a true account, and in a true account a man's mistakes have to be left where he made them, or nobody learns anything, least of all him.
I took him up the valley in the second year, to the shelf of grass, and he went quiet when he saw the stones and would not walk on that side of the stream.
Then he told me, in the broken English we had between us then, that his people knew this island.

They did not come to it. That was the point — the men in the boats came from further along the coast and his people thought them fools. But there was an old story, from before his grandfather, about a man who came to this island out of the sea in a broken boat.
The story had two details in it and both of them went through me like cold water.

The man had lived here a long time, alone. And he had gone out every morning before the sun and stood and spoken, and bowed, facing away from the place the sun came up — which is exactly what a story would remember, because on that coast it makes no sense at all.
